why.correct: She watches and records natural behavior in its real setting without intervening, which is naturalistic observation.
options: Right: she records behavior where it happens and changes nothing.
An experiment needs a variable the researcher manipulates and random assignment to conditions; she changes nothing.
A case study looks in depth at one person or a small group; she counts behavior across many strangers.
A survey asks people to report on themselves; she never asks anyone anything.

why.correct: The researchers measured two variables as they occurred. A correlational study shows that variables are related, not that one causes the other: a third variable, such as stress, could affect both.
options: Nothing was manipulated and no one was randomly assigned, so a cause cannot be claimed.
Right: this is a correlational study; it shows a relationship, not a cause.
That is one possible direction, but the data cannot show it any more than the reverse.
Self-reports can be biased, but that does not make a relationship a chance result.

why.correct: A case study examines one person (or a few) in depth. It is useful for rare conditions and for generating hypotheses, but what is true of one person may not be true of others.
options: One patient, with nothing manipulated, cannot show a general cause.
Random assignment belongs to experiments; the issue with a case study is that one person may be atypical.
Right: a case study is rich in detail and can spark hypotheses, but one patient may be unusual.
That describes a correlational study, which needs many people; this is one patient.

why.correct: A testable hypothesis is a specific prediction about how variables relate, stated so that data could support or refute it.
options: "Some kind of effect" names no direction and no measurement, so no result could clearly support or refute it.
A hypothesis is a testable statement, not a question.
"Focus" and "calm and pleasant" are not defined as measurements, and music is not mentioned.
Right: it names the groups, a measurable outcome and a direction.

why.correct: An operational definition turns a concept into the exact procedure or count used to measure it, here hits and kicks counted in 10 minutes.
options: Right: it states exactly how aggression is measured in this study.
A hypothesis predicts how variables are related; this only says how one variable is measured.
A theory is a broad explanation that organizes many findings, not a measurement rule.
A confounding variable is an unwanted difference between groups; this is the measure of the outcome.

why.correct: Only random assignment makes the groups alike, on average, in everything except the treatment. When people choose their own group, differences such as motivation can explain the result: a confounding variable.
options: The question is not about a missing hypothesis; the problem is how people got into the groups.
Right: without random assignment, motivation is a confounding variable.
Word recall can be counted; the problem is how the groups were formed.
Nothing in the stem gives group sizes; the problem is that people chose their own groups.

why.correct: When both participants and the people who collect data are unaware of the conditions, the study is double-blind. It controls participants’ expectations (placebo effects) and the researchers’ expectations (experimenter bias).
options: In a single-blind study only the participants are kept unaware; here the raters are unaware too.
Random assignment decides who gets which pill; keeping everyone unaware is blinding.
Right: neither side knows, so neither expectations nor ratings can favor one group.
An operational definition is a measurement rule; this procedure is about who knows the conditions.

why.correct: Small changes in how a question is phrased can change answers. Calling the ban "unfair" pushes respondents toward agreeing.
options: Experimenter bias is a researcher’s expectations shaping the results during data collection; here the printed question itself differs.
A placebo effect is a change caused by expecting a treatment to work; no treatment is given here.
That bias is answering to look good; the difference here comes from how the question is phrased.
Right: the loaded word "unfair" nudges people toward one answer.

why.correct: People tend to report what makes them look good, especially when someone they know is listening. Answering without giving a name reduces this self-report bias.
options: Right: face to face, students answer in the way that looks better.
The question was the same; what changed was who heard the answer.
This is about how the participants answered, not about the researcher’s expectations shaping the data.
No variable was manipulated and nothing was randomly assigned, so this is not an experiment.

why.correct: A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies of the same question, so one unusual study counts for less.
options: That is a replication.
Right: it pools many studies into one estimate.
That is peer review.
That is a case study.

why.correct: Replication is how science corrects itself. When larger, careful repeats of a study cannot reproduce its result, the original finding is doubtful.
options: Peer review checks a study’s methods; it does not guarantee that the result will hold up.
One study does not prove a result even for its own sample; and later studies with the same procedure found no effect.
Right: a finding that larger repeats cannot reproduce should not be taught as established.
Being famous is not evidence; larger studies with the same procedure count for more.

why.correct: The biological perspective looks at the body and brain; the cognitive perspective looks at how people think, remember and interpret events.
options: The behavioral perspective looks at learning from consequences, and the humanistic at growth and free choice; neither fits.
Sociocultural looks at culture and groups, psychodynamic at inner conflicts outside awareness; neither fits.
Evolutionary explanations appeal to survival and reproduction; neither explanation does.
Right: the body’s processes, then patterns of thinking.

why.correct: The independent variable is the one the researchers manipulate: here, the type of drink.
options: Right: the researchers set this for each student.
That is measured, so it is the dependent variable.
That is part of the blinding procedure, kept the same for everyone.
Age describes the participants; the researchers did not manipulate it.

why.correct: A placebo looks like the treatment but has no active ingredient. If expecting a boost made people faster, both groups would show it, so any difference left over points to the drink itself.
options: Group size is set by assignment, not by what the control group drinks.
Right: a placebo makes expectations the same in both groups.
The operational definition is the same for both groups; the placebo is about expectations.
The look-alike drink keeps the conditions hidden, not visible.

why.correct: Random assignment spreads differences such as alertness or sleep evenly across the groups, so a difference afterward can be traced to the drink.
options: Volunteering says who took part; it does not make the two groups comparable.
A precise measure is useful, but it does not by itself allow a causal claim.
Right: random assignment makes the groups alike, on average, before the drinks.
Several trials make the measure steadier; they do not make the groups comparable.

why.correct: An operational definition says exactly how this study measured the variable, with the unit and the procedure.
With random assignment the groups started out alike, so the higher average after practice questions (15 versus 11) points to the practice questions as the cause.
options: Rereading averaged 11, below the practice-question group’s 15.
Both studying groups scored well above the group that did not study (6).
Averages describe groups; the table gives no information about individual students.
Right: 15 is higher than 11, and random assignment allows a causal reading.

why.correct: A control group gets no treatment (or a placebo) and provides the baseline that shows whether the treatments made a difference.
options: Right: it gives a baseline to compare both studying groups with.
A comparison group is part of the design, not an unwanted difference.
The dependent variable is the quiz score; this is a group.
Blinding is about who knows the conditions, not about a group.

why.correct: If the two studying groups spent different amounts of time, time is a confounding variable. Holding it equal leaves the kind of studying as the only difference.
options: Choosing your own group removes random assignment and adds confounding variables.
Right: otherwise the practice group may simply have studied for a different length of time.
That would add expectation effects to the results.
That group shows whether studying helps at all; it does not need to go.

why.correct: A survey asks many people to report on themselves. Here students wrote down their own homework and sleep.
options: Nothing was manipulated and no one was assigned to a homework load.
No one watched students do homework or sleep; students reported it themselves.
Right: students reported on their own homework and sleep.
A case study looks at one person in depth; 150 students answered the same questions.

why.correct: A Likert scale asks how strongly a person agrees or disagrees with a statement, on a numbered scale.
options: Blinding is about who knows the conditions; this is a kind of rating question.
Ratings are numbers, so they are quantitative data.
A placebo is a fake treatment; nothing was given to the students.
Right: a rating of agreement with a statement.

why.correct: Self-reports depend on people’s memory and honesty, so estimates can be off, and people may report healthier habits than they have.
options: Right: self-reports are open to memory errors and social desirability bias.
Leaving names off usually makes answers more honest, not less.
Surveys can ask about behavior; the problem is how well people report it.
Nobody was assigned anything; homework load was reported, not set.

why.correct: A study starts from a hypothesis, defines how each variable will be measured, assigns people to conditions by chance, measures the outcome and then compares the groups.
In a correlational study the relationship can run either way, or a third variable (such as having more free time, or living with family) can affect both.
options: Possible: the result fits this, but the data alone cannot show it.
Possible: the direction could run the other way.
Nobody was randomly assigned a pet, so no causal claim follows.
A placebo effect comes from expecting a treatment to work; no treatment was given.

why.correct: The population is the whole group a study wants to draw conclusions about; the sample is the smaller group actually studied.
options: Right: the population is everyone the study wants to describe.
Those 300 are the sample, the part of the population actually studied.
That is a subgroup of answers, not the group the study is about.
The study is about current seniors, not all future college students.

why.correct: A convenience sample takes whoever is easy to reach. Gaming-forum users differ from teens in general, so the sample is biased no matter how many reply.
options: Random assignment matters for causal claims in experiments; the question is who the results describe.
Right: a convenience sample of forum users is unlikely to be representative.
2,000 is a large sample; size cannot fix a sample drawn from the wrong place.
The stem says nothing about the wording; the problem it describes is where the sample came from.

why.correct: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being included, which makes a representative sample likely.
options: Only students who eat in the cafeteria at that time can be chosen.
Volunteers differ from those who do not volunteer.
Right: every student has the same chance of being chosen.
Students in large classes, often required courses, may differ from others.

why.correct: Random sampling (selection) lets results generalize to the population; random assignment to conditions lets an experiment show cause and effect.
options: This swaps the two: assignment is what allows the cause-and-effect conclusion.
They do different jobs: one is about who is studied, the other about which condition each gets.
Size does not replace either step: a large biased sample is still biased.
Right: sampling decides who is studied, assignment decides which condition.

why.correct: Generalizability depends on how similar the participants are to the group you want to describe: here, age and type of school differ.
options: Right: it argues from participant characteristics, both sides.
Generalizing depends on who the participants were, not on the count alone.
Random assignment supports a causal claim for these participants; it says nothing about other ages.
Ages, schooling and backgrounds differ; a claim about everyone needs evidence from different groups.

why.correct: People who choose to respond often care more about the issue than others, so a self-selected sample does not represent the population.
options: An operational definition is a measurement rule; the problem is who called.
Right: a self-selected sample is a biased sample.
Blinding belongs to experiments; this is about who is in the sample.
A percent of callers is a description of a sample, and the problem is the sample.

why.correct: Random selection gave every ad responder the same chance, so the sample represents the people who answered the ad, not adults in general.
options: Nobody outside the people who answered the ad could be chosen.
That is one condition of the experiment, not the population.
Right: the 120 were chosen at random from those 300 people.
Many were retired, but the pool was one city’s ad responders.

why.correct: Generalizability is argued from participant characteristics, such as age and life situation, compared with the group you want to describe.
options: Random assignment supports the causal claim; it does not limit generalizing.
The measure applies to anyone; the participants’ characteristics are the issue.
Duration is a design feature; the question asks about who the participants were.
Right: their age and daily life differ from teenagers’.

why.correct: A generalizability answer names the population and supports the claim with specific characteristics of the participants.
Compare each row: a share among respondents far above the town’s share means overrepresented; far below means underrepresented.
options: Right: 55% versus 20% for ages 18 to 29, and 3% versus 15% for 70 and older.
Every age group differs, some by more than 30 points.
The two oldest groups make up a smaller share of respondents than of the town.
They make up 30% of respondents, close to their 35% of the town.

why.correct: An online survey that mostly reached young adults is a biased sample, so its results describe young respondents more than the town.
options: Surveys can ask about sleep; the problem here is who answered.
Right: a sample that misrepresents the population cannot describe it.
Surveys produce descriptive results; the issue is the sample.
The measure is clear enough; the problem is who answered.

why.correct: Random sampling from a list of the whole population gives every adult the same chance of being chosen, so all age groups appear in about their true shares.
options: More replies from the same kind of respondents does not fix the bias.
Friends of young respondents are likely to be young too.
Right: random sampling from the whole population.
Random assignment compares conditions; it does not change who is in the sample.

why.correct: Strength is the size of r, ignoring the sign. A coefficient near -1 or +1 is strong; near 0 is weak.
options: Right: its size, 0.82, is the largest; the minus sign gives only the direction.
Its size, 0.45, is smaller than 0.82.
This is close to zero: a very weak relationship.
Its size, 0.30, is smaller than 0.82.

why.correct: Two variables can move together because a third variable affects both. Hot months bring more swimming (and drownings) and more ice cream.
options: A correlation does not show cause; a third variable explains this one.
Right: summer heat drives both.
That reverses the direction, and it still ignores the obvious third variable.
An illusory correlation is a relationship people believe in that the data do not show; here the data show one.

why.correct: A correlational finding does not justify "boosts". Families with regular routines may provide both breakfast and support for schoolwork.
options: Higher grades with breakfast is a positive correlation, not a negative one.
Any two measured variables can be correlated.
Right: a third variable, such as a structured home life, may explain both.
A correlation proves no cause, including sleep.

why.correct: When one variable goes up as the other goes down, the correlation is negative.
options: A positive r means both rise together; here one falls as the other rises.
Zero means no relationship; these two clearly move together.
r is always between -1 and +1, so 1.50 is impossible.
Right: as one rises the other falls, and the link is fairly strong.

why.correct: The directionality problem: in a correlation we cannot tell which of the two variables affects the other.
options: Right: aggression could lead to game choice, the reverse of the usual story.
That is a third variable, a separate problem from directionality.
That is a source of bias in the measure, not directionality.
That limits generalizing; it is not about which variable came first.

why.correct: An illusory correlation is a relationship people believe in that the data do not show, often because memorable cases stand out.
options: The records show no relationship at all, positive or negative.
Right: people remember the cases that fit their belief.
There is no relationship in the records for a third variable to explain.
Experimenter bias is a researcher’s expectations shaping the data; here the records are accurate and the error is in the nurse’s memory.

why.correct: A positive correlation means the two variables move in the same direction, both up or both down together.
options: Right: both rise together.
Practice rises as mistakes fall: negative.
Both fall together, which is also positive.
No relationship: r near zero.

why.correct: The points slope upward and cluster tightly around the line of best fit: strong and positive. For these invented data r = .88.
options: The points rise from left to right, so the correlation is positive.
The points sit close to the line, so the relationship is strong.
Right: scores rise with hours and the points lie close to the line (r = .88).
There is a clear upward pattern.

why.correct: The students chose how much to study, so this is a correlational study. Interest, prior knowledge or free time could affect both hours and scores. An experiment that randomly assigns study time would be needed to show cause.
options: The points rise from left to right: the correlation is positive.
There is a clear, strong pattern.
A scatterplot shows a relationship, never a cause, whatever its size.
Right: a third variable, such as interest, could explain the pattern.

why.correct: The line of best fit passes near 70 at 4 hours. A correlation lets you predict one variable from the other, even though it does not show cause.
options: Right: the line passes near 70 at 4 hours.
That is near the line at 1 hour.
That is near the line at 8 hours.
That is the number of hours, not a score.

why.correct: Name the direction and strength, then say what the correlation does and does not show.
Compare the size of r without the sign: 0.71 is the largest.
options: Its size, 0.62, is moderate and smaller than 0.71.
Right: 0.71 is the largest size in the table.
0.31 is a weak relationship.
0.18 is weak.

why.correct: The sign gives the direction (negative: as one rises, the other tends to fall); the size, 0.62, says the relationship is moderately strong.
options: That would be a positive correlation.
r is not a percent, and a correlation does not show cause.
Right: a negative r means one tends to fall as the other rises.
An r of -0.62 is a moderate relationship, well away from zero.

why.correct: Even a strong correlation cannot show which variable affects the other, or rule out a third variable such as boredom or anxiety.
options: Strength does not turn a correlation into a cause.
The r is +0.71, positive.
A large sample does not show cause either.
Right: the directionality problem, plus possible third variables.

why.correct: An institutional review board reviews research plans before data collection to protect the participants’ rights and welfare.
options: Right: an IRB reviews and approves research with human participants.
Peer review checks a finished study before publication, not a plan before it starts.
A control group is part of a study’s design, not a review committee.
Debriefing happens with participants after the study.

why.correct: Minors cannot give legal consent, so a parent or guardian consents and the minor gives assent: their own agreement after the study is explained in terms they understand.
options: Debriefing explains the study afterward; it is not agreement to take part.
Right: a minor’s own agreement, given alongside a parent’s consent.
Confidentiality protects participants’ data, not their agreement.
Peer review is experts checking a study for a journal.

why.correct: Participants can withdraw at any point without losing anything they were promised.
options: Nothing in the stem says the study involved deception or explained it.
Confidentiality is about protecting records, not about leaving.
Right: participants may stop at any time without penalty.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.

why.correct: When a study uses deception, ethics codes require debriefing: telling participants the truth and the reason for the deception as soon as possible.
options: Consent comes before the study, and here the true purpose was hidden at that point.
Peer review is experts evaluating the study for a journal.
Blinding hides conditions during the study; this step reveals the purpose after it.
Right: explaining the study, and any deception, after participation.

why.correct: Confidentiality means information about participants is kept private and their identities are protected.
options: Right: participants’ identities and data are kept private.
Assent is a minor’s agreement to take part.
Harm is about physical or emotional risk during the study; this is about records.
Debriefing explains the study after it ends.

why.correct: An ethics answer must name a safeguard the summary describes (consent, withdrawal, confidentiality, debriefing, IRB approval, protection from harm) and say how it was applied.
options: Random assignment is used in experiments.
Right: readers do not accept design features as ethics.
Any safeguard the summary describes can earn the point if its use is explained.
Ethical guidelines protect both human and animal participants.

why.correct: Animal research must be approved by a committee that checks housing, care, pain control and whether the use of animals is justified.
options: Animals cannot consent; their welfare is protected by committee review.
Debriefing is for people, explaining the study after it ends.
Right: animal research is reviewed for humane care and justified use.
Confidentiality protects people’s identities, not lab animals’.

why.correct: The speech was a cover story. Deception is allowed only when the study needs it, the risk is small and participants are debriefed.
options: Random assignment is a design feature, not deception.
That is the measure, recorded honestly.
Consent is a safeguard, not deception.
Right: the students were misled about the speech.

why.correct: Name a safeguard the summary describes, then say exactly how these researchers carried it out.
Informed consent means knowing what participation involves. The cover story kept the speech threat out of the form, which is why debriefing was required.
options: Right: the stressful part was not described in advance.
Saying participants may withdraw is part of proper consent.
Review board approval supports the study’s ethics.
Assignment is a design feature unrelated to consent.

why.correct: Protection from harm means keeping risks minimal: a short, mild source of stress with a full explanation before participants leave.
options: That is a result, not a protection.
Right: the stress was short and resolved before students left.
The number and ages of participants do not reduce harm.
The task’s length does not address the stress.

why.correct: Institutional review board approval happens before data collection: the board checks the plan, including the deception and the debriefing.
options: Debriefing came at the end of each session.
That is the measure, given during the session.
Right: the summary says the IRB approved the study.
Assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.

In order: 3, 4, 7, 9, 15. The middle (third) value is 7.

With six values, the median is halfway between the two middle values: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>7.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6 + 9}{2} = 7.5</annotation></semantics></math> minutes.
9 appears three times, more than any other rating.

Range = highest minus lowest: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19 - 5 = 14</annotation></semantics></math> seconds.
The standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of scores from the mean. A standard deviation of 15 means scores are much more spread out than with 4.
options: Right: a larger standard deviation means more variation.
Both means are 75, so neither scored higher on average.
Standard deviation measures spread, not the number of students.
A larger standard deviation usually goes with a larger range, not a smaller one.

why.correct: Outliers pull the mean toward them. In a skewed distribution, the median better describes the typical case.
options: Using every value is why the few billionaires pull it far up.
Right: the median depends on the middle, not the extremes.
The range measures spread, not a typical value.
Standard deviation measures spread, not a typical value.

why.correct: A bimodal distribution has two peaks. It often means two different groups are mixed together, such as students who did and did not read the assigned book.
options: A symmetric distribution with one peak has a single hump in the middle.
Skew is one peak with a long tail on one side.
Right: two modes, two peaks.
Skew is one peak with a long tail on one side.

why.correct: The standard deviation measures variation. A value of 0.5 means almost everyone recalled between 11 and 13 words.
options: The mean is 12; the 0.5 describes spread around it.
Standard deviation is about spread, not sample size.
Outliers would make the standard deviation larger, not smaller.
Right: a small standard deviation means scores sit close to the mean.

why.correct: Total: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>280</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2(280)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>300</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 4(300)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>320</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 3(320)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>900</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 900</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>560</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 560</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>1200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 1200</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>960</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 960</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mn>900</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ 900</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>3620</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 3620</annotation></semantics></math>. Mean: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>3620</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>362</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3620}{10} = 362</annotation></semantics></math> ms.
In order: 280, 280, 300, 300, 300, 300, 320, 320, 320, 900. The two middle values (5th and 6th) are both 300, so the median is 300 ms.
The median (300 ms) sits with the typical trials; the mean (362 ms) is higher than nine of the ten trials because of a single outlier.
options: Right: one outlier moves the mean far more than the median.
Including the outlier is exactly why the mean misleads here.
The range describes spread, not a usual value.
The mode is 300 and the mean is 362; they are not equal.

why.correct: Range = highest minus lowest: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>900</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>280</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>620</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">900 - 280 = 620</annotation></semantics></math> ms.

Without the outlier, the mean is <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2720</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>302</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2720}{9} \approx 302</annotation></semantics></math> ms; the median of the nine remaining trials is the 5th value, 300 ms. The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is not.
options: The mean falls by about 60 ms; the median does not change.
Right: the mean falls to about 302 ms, and the middle of the nine values is still 300.
This reverses the effect: the mean is the measure sensitive to outliers.
One extreme trial changes the mean a great deal.

why.correct: The tail points toward the low scores, so the distribution is negatively skewed. Easy tests often produce this shape.
options: A positive skew has its tail toward the high values; this tail points to the low scores.
There is one peak, from 80 to 90.
Right: most scores are high, with a tail stretching toward the low scores.
A symmetric distribution has matching sides; this one has a tail on the left.

why.correct: The mean is pulled toward the tail. With a tail of low scores (negative skew), the mean falls below the median.
options: That is the pattern for a positive skew, with a tail of high values.
They are equal in a symmetric distribution, not a skewed one.
The mode is in the 80 to 90 bin and the median is in the same region.
Right: the few low scores pull the mean down toward the tail.

why.correct: The tallest bar of a histogram is the most frequent range: here 80 to 90, with 8 students.
options: Right: 8 students, the tallest bar.
That bar holds 5 students.
